content.thinking:
I'm avoiding the existing red panda samples and designing this scene from scratch — a Genshin-style red panda perched on a mossy boulder, working out realistic proportions for both the animal and the stone so the pose feels balanced and natural.

For the rig, I'm deciding the stone needs its own root joint rather than treating the panda as the sole skeleton — a base joint at the stone's center with the panda's hips as a child, so the stone geometry can ride along with the base transform while the panda poses independently with a wide, planted stance and an arched tail for visual balance.

Now I'm working out the stone's construction: a lumpy boulder built from a lathe profile with faceted segments, cel-shaded with a painted moss patch on the upper surface determined by surface normal and noise, giving it a toon two-tone look. I'm placing the panda's paws on a flattened plateau near the top of the stone around y=0.25–0.26, sizing the boulder's radius to roughly 0.22 meters to match that resting surface.

Writing the rock geometry displacement...

Now I'm thinking through red panda anatomy for the design: long body, bushy ringed tail, round head with white-edged ears, tear-mark stripes, cream-white face markings, rusty-red back with dark belly and legs, rendered in a Genshin-style cel-shaded anime look with gold trinket accents and an elemental glow effect.

I'm settling on a Dendro-themed accessory set — a small gold bell collar with tassel, a leaf-shaped charm on a red cord with a glowing dendro gem, and a mossy stone base with tiny glowing mushrooms and floating dendro motes for subtle elemental flair, keeping the loose floating bits minimal so nothing awkwardly hovers. Now I'm working out the panda's body proportions, starting with chest-to-rump length.

For sizing I'm going chunkier and more stylized with a bigger head, landing on roughly 0.55m head-body length, and sketching stone dimensions (0.7 long x 0.55 wide x 0.24 tall) with a plateau for the paws to rest on, spacing front and hind paw positions symmetrically. For the pose, I'm aiming for a balancing stance — wide-set paws gripping a smaller stone top (~0.4), tail swept up in an S-curve, body slightly lifted rather than a fully neutral rest pose.

Now I'm laying out the skeleton: a root base, hips joint, and a spine chain running from hips through mid-body to chest, then neck to head, with a separate tail chain branching off the hips. I'm planning to sweep the body geometry along this spine using varying radius values for a thick, rounded build, considering whether to loft the tail into the same continuous path or keep it as its own overlapping sweep for simplicity.

For the ground contact, I'm clamping the stone's bottom vertices so they sit almost exactly at y=0, computing the local displacement needed given its scale and center so the sink stays under 2%. I'm also tallying up the panda's overall height by stacking paw, shoulder, head, and ear heights to estimate the total silhouette size including a raised tail.

For the legs, I'm sketching out a short, stubby limb structure typical of a real red panda: a shoulder joint, elbow, and wrist chain with small segment lengths so the paws just reach the ground from the body's underside.

For hind legs I'm using knee hint pointing forward, then extending to ankle with similar segment lengths, with a flat plantigrade paw extending forward from the ankle to match the target height.

For the paws themselves, I'm planning a tapered sweep with ellipsoid pads and small toe bumps with tiny claws for the red panda look, rigging each paw with a few digit joints parented to the tip, keeping the joint count well under budget.

Now I'm sketching out the head: a round skull sphere widened at the cheeks, positioned and aimed forward, with cheek tufts to follow.

For the eyes, I'm using animeEye decals sized large on the face, deciding between a warm amber-gold iris or a brighter stylized green, leaning toward a gentle green-gold blend for that anime look rather than realistic dark red panda eyes.

For the facial markings, I'm working out how to paint the characteristic red panda face pattern using local coordinates relative to the head center—white eyebrow patches above the eyes, white cheeks and muzzle, and dark tear-stripe marks running from the inner eye corners down toward the mouth, layered over the rust-colored base fur.

Now I'm figuring out the body's color scheme and shading: a bright rust-orange back fading to dark chestnut/black on the belly and legs, with a toon-style cel shading function to derive lit and shadowed tones for each region.

For the tail I'm planning alternating lighter and darker rust rings along its length, with zigzagged edges so the bands don't look perfectly straight, using the tail's sweep position to determine ring placement.

For the stone and setting I'm settling on a blue-grey stone with violet shadows, vivid green moss with lighter highlights, and gold trim accents. For ornaments, I'm thinking of a thin red cord collar with a gold leaf-shaped pendant holding a glowing green gem plus a small tassel, and possibly a gold band around the tail base with a hanging tassel too.

Actually I'll shift the tail ornament to a gold ear cuff on the left ear with a tassel and green gem for that Genshin feel. For the stone itself, I'm adding a carved ruins rim with gold inlay, a glowing dendro sprout, tiny glowing mushrooms, floating light motes, and small white sweet flowers with yellow centers, plus droopy moss tufts along the edge and some ground clutter to anchor the base.

For fur, I'm layering tapering flame-shaped tufts as tinted cards across the cheeks, chest ruff, tail fluff, leg fringes, and haunches, with tint read once per card from the paint at the root using the frame's normal axis rather than full cel shading. Now I'm thinking through how to build out the big bushy tail shape.

Still writing tail geometry...

Still working out the chain structure...

Radii taper from rump to chest to neck, with a slight downward shift for belly sag, and I'm checking that leg clearance between belly and ground stays reasonable for a chunky animal. For painting, I'm applying countershading with a furry edge transition between rust on top and darker belly fur below, using a ragged boundary with some period and tooth parameters along the body.

Now I'm sketching the head geometry: a skull sphere positioned above the head joint, scaled wider than tall for that chunky chibi look, with a short blunt snout sphere offset forward and a dark nose tip, plus a small lower jaw ellipsoid attached to its own joint for articulation.

I'm planning the facial paint logic next, mapping local coordinates relative to the head center to lay down a rust-colored crown, a lighter rust forehead patch, and white cheek regions based on position thresholds.

Still refining facial markings...

Now I'm working out eye placement as decals on the skull surface, using azimuth and elevation angles to position the anime-style eye texture relative to face size, while mirroring correctly for the left side and deciding whether to keep default blush and brow styling.

For ears, I'm planning an extruded rounded-triangle outline standing on the top-sides of the head, orienting the extrusion axes so the ear face points forward with thickness running front-to-back, and tilting the ear outward slightly along its vertical axis.

Still shaping the ear outline...

For the inner ear I'm layering a smaller cream-colored patch slightly in front, with a softer plum-pink crescent near the base and a bit of white fluffy fur detail inside to sell that red panda look.

Now I'm adding cheek tufts — three small white spike shapes per side, positioned along the cheek and pointing outward along the surface normal, painted with the cream tone to match the cel-shaded style.

I'm weighing texture resolution tradeoffs: a 1024 atlas gives roughly 1.3mm per texel over the body surface, which should be plenty crisp for tear marks and fine cel-ink lines without needing a heavier 2048 or 4096 atlas. I'll stick with 1024 as the default and move on to texturing the fur tuft cards with tinted colors.

Writing fur tuft SVG...

Now I'm sketching the overall card count (~150 on the body, ~120 on the tail, each cheap at 4 triangles) and starting to work out the rock geometry—thinking about using a displaced icosahedron scaled anisotropically, and placing the panda's front and hind paw positions along the z-axis to establish footprint spacing.

I'm iterating on the clamp value for flattening the icosahedron's top to form a plateau, checking that the resulting flat radius is wide enough for the front paws to stand without falling off the sloped edge, adjusting the y-scale and clamp threshold until the plateau geometry comfortably covers the paw footprint.

That gives a squat barrel-shaped stone with flat plateau roughly 0.26 x 0.21 at top and bottom, like a mossy pillar stump. I'll place the panda's paws on that plateau—front paws around z=0.17, hind around z=-0.15—keeping them within the stone's bounds.

I also want to scatter secondary rocks around the base: a few small flattened icosahedron boulders and a pebble ring, plus a bigger moss-topped rock lower step at back-left and front-right to build out the diorama, making sure none exceed y>0.25 to avoid clashing with the tail. For the moss coloring, I'm defining a function that blends mossy green tones onto the rock surface based on noise and surface normal (favoring upward-facing areas), using stone colors like "#9aa3b8" alongside moss greens "#7ed957" and a darker moss variant.

For shading I'm wrapping the paint into a cel-shading function, deriving shadows from the resolved color, and adding dark crack lines across the stone for texture. I thought about adding a carved glyph ring or glowing crystal accents but decided to skip the extra decoration and keep the stone simple with moss and flowers instead, to stay within a budget of roughly 400-600 total parts. Now I'm sketching out the full skeleton and body part list—root, hips, spine segments, neck, head, jaw, and ear joints—to start assembling the character structure.

I'm tallying up joint counts across the body: tail chain, four legs each with multiple spans and toe digits, ears, and jaw, landing around 40 joints total, while deciding how many toes to give each paw for a readable but not overly complex result, favoring three slightly larger toes per paw over four smaller ones for clarity at this scale.

Now I'm sketching shoulder and haunch bulges using sphere blobs on the hip joints to suggest thigh volume, skipping a dorsal stripe to keep the Genshin-style simplicity, and planning an anime-style face with big eyes, blush cheeks, a small nose, and a "w"-shaped mouth. For accents, I'm designing a red cord collar with a gold pendant shaped like a leaf or droplet holding a glowing green gem, plus a hanging tassel with gold and teal strands.

I'm adding more ornate details: a gold ear cuff torus with a hanging tassel and gem on the left ear, a gold band with a dangling tassel near the tail tip, and tiny gold bangles with teal beads on both front wrists for a cute touch. I'm also planning glowing elements like the gem pendant and a dendro sprout with a glowing leaf.

Then I'm scattering small floating glow motes (green/gold octahedra) around the panda, adding tiny glowing mushroom caps on the stone, plus moss strand cards hanging from the stone edges and grass tufts placed around the stone base on the ground.

Now I'm planning white-petaled flower cards with yellow centers scattered on the stone shoulder and ground, plus moss leaf cards and lathe-built mushroom caps with stems — and considering whether toon ink outlines should apply to fur edges rather than the stone itself, before moving on to concrete toe and claw geometry using local joint orientation helpers.

Before coding, I'm mapping out the builder API's function signatures — sweep, chain, joint, part, stick, surface, decal, cards, spike, capsule, rod, extrude, lathe — and settling on a mirroring convention where +X represents the left side in absolute coordinates, so I can loop through sides consistently when building symmetric parts.

Now I'm planning the skeleton layout: hip position at roughly [0, 0.405, -0.19], a spine chain running through a few points to give the chunky body a slight arch, and figuring out whether hips should be a dedicated root joint or just the first spine joint, since the stone/base part also needs a root to attach to.

Actually, I'll fold hips directly into the spine chain as its first joint, naming the chain "spine" with members hips, spine2, chest, parented to a base root—giving three spans from the four points.

Then I'll add a neck chain from chest tip to a neck joint, and a separate head joint parented to the neck, aiming forward and up. For the body silhouette, I'm sketching a catmull-rom path running from the rump through the hip and spine region up into the chest and neck, mapping those points onto the hips/spine/chest bones for the sweep.

I'm defining a radius profile along that body path—small at the rump, swelling through the mid-back, then tapering toward the neck—with matching rx/ry values and smooth circular cross-sections for a chunky, rounded look. Now I'm thinking about how to add fur ruff detailing at the neck/shoulders and deciding on a cream-white chest coloring consistent with a red panda's markings.

Positioning the skull sphere so it sits just behind the chest with enough radius to overlap the neck's end cleanly. Working out shoulder, wrist, and paw joint positions and limb thickness so the legs look proportionate and the front paws rest naturally on top of the stone surface without clipping through it.

Laying out the front paw's toe structure now—placing three toe chains with forward-pointing tips and small rounded radii, positioned just ahead of the paw center so they read as distinct digits resting on the stone.

Now I'm figuring out the hind leg: hip socket, thigh blob, knee bend hint, and a plantigrade ankle-to-paw layout so the hind foot sits flatter and longer than the front, with toes extending forward from the heel.

For the joint chains, I'm naming hip/knee/ankle for the hind legs and shoulder/elbow/wrist for the front, and deciding whether to label the forelimb chains as "arm" or "leg" roles given this is a quadruped rig.

Settling on using "leg" for all four limbs since that's standard for quadrupeds, with toes parented to the chain tips and uniquely named per side. Now I'm sketching the tail's joint path from the hips outward and upward, mapping out six control points that curve the tail up and back, though the resulting height might end up taller than intended.

Since a standing red panda's tail would hang rather than curl high, I'm softening the curve by adjusting the later points downward for a more natural ~0.7 overall height, and defining a tapering radius profile across the six tail segments with a rounded, blunt tip matching the real animal's coloring.

Now I'm defining the ring pattern paint function — alternating rust and darker brown bands along the tail length using a zigzag offset, with the final tip segment switching to a near-black dark tone. I'm also adding scattered fluffy edge cards along the tail silhouette, tinted using the same ring coloring sampled at the root frame so the fuzz matches the banding underneath.

Realizing the paint function needs a proper coordinate to sample from, I switch to using the path's closestT method to find each point's position along the tail curve directly, which works cleanly for both the texture bake and the edge cards, then I wiggle the band boundaries slightly based on position to make them look more organic rather than perfectly straight rings.

Now I'm working out the facial features: cel-shaded cream coloring for the snout and jaw, dark flat color for the nose, and figuring out how to draw the mouth line — settling on a small dark rod running as a philtrum from the nose down to the mouth center as a simpler alternative to a swept path.

Jaw joint aims toward a lower jaw piece, a small cream-painted scaled sphere beneath the snout, kept closed with no teeth or tongue needed. For whiskers, I'll add three thin spike-like rods per side on the snout.

Still writing whisker and ear placement code...

I'm checking the cross product to confirm which way the ear's thickness axis points, since mirroring with s=1 vs s=-1 flips the face toward +Z or -Z — I need to make sure the orientation stays consistent for both sides.

Adjusting the ear basis vectors for shear...

Computing the cross product gives the front-facing normal direction, which I'll use to decide fur coloring on the ear — front faces with normal component above a threshold get white inner fur, otherwise rust, with a rim boundary based on whether the point falls inside the inner outline.

I'm defining the inner white region using a scaled, zigzag-fuzzy outline so the border looks like fur texture rather than a clean edge, with rust forming the rim around it and covering the entire back face, then considering whether to add a white tuft card at the ear base.

Now I'm adding small white spike clusters inside the ear base for the inner tuft, plus neck ruff, cheek, and forehead fur tufts using cone shapes, and scattering fur cards on the body that read their tint from the surface normal so they shade correctly above and below the fur edge.

For the body I'm scattering around 140 fur card hits with a minimum distance, filtering out ones facing too far downward, giving them a backward-and-down flow direction, a varied size range, and a steep lean so they create a jagged tufted silhouette from the sides, plus extra cards for the chest ruff and cheeks. Then I'm setting the pendant gem to glow emissive green and placing a handful of small glowing diamond-shaped motes floating around the panda at a modest height off the ground.

I'm keeping total bounding height under control while adding a small dendro sprout with glowing green-teal leaves near a stone at the back-left, plus a trio of glowing mushrooms at the stone's base on the other side. For the stone itself, I want carved rune-like groove patterns on its visible faces, so rather than relying on paint (which can't glow) I'm planning to decal a glowing teal rune texture plane onto the stone surface instead.

I'm placing two rune decals on the stone's visible front-left and right-back faces, using a design that's a gold circle outline with an inscribed glowing teal leaf glyph -- generic enough to avoid referencing any specific game's emblem. I also want a mossy, cracked overlay using noise for added texture realism.

Now I'm writing the rock geometry generator function that takes a seed and dimensions and returns displaced geometry, with lower detail (icosahedron, ~80 faces) for small rocks and higher detail (~320 faces) for the main stone, plus a flat-shading flag for faceted normals.

For displacement I'm using a deterministic sine-based pseudo-noise function based on vertex position so shared vertices stay coincident, scaling each vertex outward by roughly 12% variation, then clamping the y-coordinate after scaling so the bottom sits flush at y=0 and the top caps at a fixed height. I'm baking the final world coordinates directly into the main stone's geometry rather than relying on scale/position options in the part placement.

For the mossy top, I'm making the entire flat plateau face green via the normal direction, adding scattered moss patches on the sides based on noise, and placing small flattened green blob clumps along the plateau edges to soften the rim while keeping them clear of the panda's paw placements.

Checking the geometry though, I realize the plateau is too small — the front paws extend past its edge at z=0.28 while the plateau only reaches z=0.2. I need to enlarge the plateau scale to roughly [0.42, 0.17, 0.36] and reposition the front paws closer to z=0.20 so they stay fully supported on the surface.

That's borderline given the random displacement, so I'll pull the panda stance in tighter: front paws centered at z 0.16 with toes to 0.215, hind paws heel at z -0.20 with toes to -0.10, keeping the body centered so the plateau at z ±0.24 still works.

Checking the shoulder-to-wrist distance comes out to about 0.128, which feels right for the arm proportions. Tracing the spine path from chest to neck to head, the skull ends up projecting forward to about z 0.35-0.38 with the snout, so the head extends nicely past the stone's front edge for a cute forward-facing look, while the rump sits around z -0.25 with hips at -0.17.

Now I'm working out the hind leg and tail placement: ankle, heel, and toe positions for the back paws, then laying out the spine chain points from hips through neck, and plotting the tail's curve from the base outward and upward into a rising arc.

I'm adding scattered stones and pebbles around the base, each defined by position, scale, and a seed for irregularity, with their bottoms clamped flush to the ground plane.

Working out the scale values gives sx 0.40, sz 0.34, so the clamped radius produces a flat plateau roughly 0.286 by 0.243 at the top, which creates the flattened appearance I want with the detail-2 icosphere clamping. Now I'm moving on to writing the moss paint function.

Defining moss coverage...

Noise handles cracks by darkening cells with steep elevation drops, and the colour functions get wrapped so each point receives a shadow tone based on its normal relative to the key light. I'm setting rock meshes to use flat normals rather than smooth shading, since that suits their faceted look better.

For the eye decals, I'm working out the skull sphere's scale and center position so I can place the eyes at the correct azimuth and elevation, then deciding between a warm gold or a cooler emerald iris color for better contrast against the orange tones elsewhere.

Now I'm settling on a teal-green iris with a lighter mint highlight, then moving to the tear marks and white facial paint, which I'm mapping directly onto the skull sphere's surface since they're flat decals. For the cheek fur, I'm planning small white cone spikes arranged in sets on each side of the head, angled outward along the surface normal at varying azimuths and elevations to create a layered fur tuft effect.

I'm leaning toward using flat cards instead for the cheek fur, scattering them across a filtered region of the skull's side surface and tinting them with a cel-shaded cream paint so the lighting stays consistent with the two-tone style rather than looking flat-lit and out of place. With that resolved, I'm moving on to designing the glow accessories, starting with a gem pendant.

I'm shaping a gold leaf extrusion with a beveled oval outline and cel-shading it in warm gold tones, then positioning the pendant on the chest and building a cord loop around the neck that follows the neck joint's orientation, tinted red and swept to a small radius. I still need to figure out exactly where the pendant hangs along the front-bottom of that loop, considering a surface ray cast from the chest area to find the right attachment point.

Below the collar, I'm computing the pendant's resting position by casting a ray from the front of the chest downward, then adjusting slightly so it sits just beneath the neck loop and tangent to the curved chest surface. I'm also planning a tassel of thin colored cords with beads hanging from the pendant's base, plus a gold ear cuff shaped as a small torus fitted around the lower rim of the ear.

Working out the cuff's exact placement and orientation on the ear...

Now I'm figuring out the tassel's hang position in world space, making sure it dangles freely below the ear ring without clipping through the head.

I'm also setting up a gold band and tassel looped around the tail at around 70% of its length, using the tail's frame to orient a swept circular path for the band thickness.

Next I'm planning a bottom-hanging tassel attachment on that same band, then moving to wrist bangles on the front legs by locating a point partway up the leg sweep chain to loop a similar ring around.

For the pendant, I'm deciding to make it a flat textured plane with an SVG-drawn gold filigree pattern—a leaf shape with swirling decorative lines and a separate glowing green gem circle layered on top, so the ornate texture stays flat while the gem gets its own glow effect.

Writing SVG shapes...

Realizing the moss clump drawn with root at bottom and tips pointing up works the same way as the grass tuft, so I can reuse that same texture for both.

Now I'm sketching color variants: grass in blue-green tones, moss in lime. For the flower card, I'm laying out a stem rising from the bottom of the canvas with five white petals tipped in pink and a yellow center clustered near the top, then moving on to a sprouting leaf design.

For the tassel, I'm figuring out the hanging orientation — since the card displays flipped when attached, I need to draw the knot near the bottom of the SVG so the strands fan out correctly once hung, which means thinking through how the drawing's edges map to the final upside-down presentation.

I'm also tallying up smaller details like whiskers, blush accents, chin fur, and paw pad colors, deciding which minor features like fangs or toe bean highlights to skip to keep the part count manageable.

For legs, I'm defining a cel-shaded gradient from dark brown at the base to rust near the shoulder, using a zigzag boundary function to make the fur transition look painterly rather than a flat line, and applying the same approach to shoulder and hip fur blobs for continuity.

Now I'm working on the body's belly-to-side color blend, using a fur edge function based on surface normal so the rust tone covers the upper sides while the belly stays dark, and deciding the chin stays white while the neck and throat keep the rust coloring rather than going pale.

I'm adding a subtle darker rust saddle streak along the spine using a small zigzag mask tied to position and normal direction, then extending similar coat painting to the leg and thigh spheres for consistency. I'm also setting up surface queries so the body sweep geometry can be properly sampled for sticking details like hits and paint.

Now I'm tallying up the full part count for the creature build — rocks, moss clumps, grass and flower cards, mushrooms, sprouts, motes, runes, and then all the body components: body sections, tail, legs, toes with claws, paws, thighs, shoulders, skull, snout, nose, jaw, eyes, and ears — to get a sense of the total piece budget before finalizing.

Beyond the core anatomy, I want to add small story-rich details: fallen leaves, tiny white flowers, dew-drop glows, freckles, forehead markings, and scattered pebbles to make the scene feel lived-in. I'm also sketching out how the cards flow for the body silhouette and planning the decal placement for the eyes using a hit-location approach with sizing and mirroring.

Writing helper for surface hits...

For the mouth, I'm deciding to keep the jaw simple -- a smaller white ellipsoid beneath the snout -- and draw the mouth as a thin dark swept line using catmull-interpolated points for the corners and center, positioned just inside the snout surface.

The mouth line where the upper snout meets the jaw stays a fine dark crease for readability. For the nose, I'm placing a small scaled sphere at the front-center of the upper snout, checking its surface z-position aligns with the skin there.

For head details I'm adding forehead rust tufts, keeping shading consistent with the cel-shaded style across flat-color elements like cords and claws. For the tail, I'm scattering fur cards along its sweep with the flow oriented toward the tip, tinted by the tail's ring paint color without additional cel shading since the ring colors are already lit.

I'm defining a shared ring color function based on position, then using the same cel-shaded paint instance for both the tail sweep and the fur card tints so they stay consistent, reading position and normal at each card's root. Body cards use the same coat paint approach as the body sweep for consistency.

Writing rock geometry function...

Still writing displacement math...

Adding a cy offset parameter to raise moss clumps so they sit near the plateau edge at roughly y=0.25, keeping their tops around 0.275.

For the paint functions, I'm using a mottled blend of two greens for the moss texture and a similar cel-shaded paint approach for stone, then setting up positions for the decorative motes. I'm also sketching a small rune decal SVG with a 64x64 viewbox and thin stroke width.

For the rune itself, I'm drawing an outer teal ring, a dashed inner ring, and a leaf-shaped glyph with a midrib and surrounding dots, using a gold-and-teal palette for a glowing effect. Then I'm figuring out how to decal this rune onto the stone surface, placing it at a hit point and orienting it to match the surface normal.

I'm placing a few decals around the stone at different azimuths — maybe front, left, and a 3/4-angle position — sized small so they fit within the visible facets, with glow strength around 1.2 so they read as glowing runes against the panda scene.

Now I'm moving on to the second rock's sprout: a small stem curving upward from near the top of Rock B with a tapered radius, and a couple of glowing leaf extrusions. I'm working out the orientation vectors so each leaf's cross-section plane is perpendicular to its growth direction and angles outward realistically from the stem tip.

I'm also topping it with a small glowing bud sphere, then shifting to designing three mushrooms near the base of the right-front rock using lathe-generated dome caps with teal glow coloring and cream stems, plus scattering a handful of tiny glowing octahedron motes around the panda for extra sparkle.

Now I'm double-checking the overall bounding box so nothing floats above the scene unexpectedly, and confirming everything touches the ground plane correctly—stones, rocks, and mushroom stems all rooted at y=0. Then I'm laying out a ring of grass tuft cards around the base, positioned to avoid overlapping the rocks, with leaning and cross-faced billboards for natural coverage.

I'm adding a low turf mound as a grounding element beneath the stone—a lathed shape rising slightly from y=0, painted with mottled moss coloring, so the rocks and grass visually sit within it rather than floating on bare ground.

Now I'm setting up the imports and constants for the actual build, pulling in the builder, frame, paint/toon utilities, and limb/IK helpers, being careful to only import what's actually used to satisfy TypeScript's strict unused-variable checks. Writing imports and constants...

Defining coat pattern logic...

I should check how shadow coloring interacts with ink edges, and verify furEdge's argument order for nested paint resolution by reading the rest of toon.ts.

input.command: cd ~/tmp-archive/sonnet-100/redPandaSonnet && sed -n 84,178p kits/toon.ts; grep -n "closestT" -n src/path.ts | head -3
